title: Bell and Choir
premise: Ulyana Coldharbour returns to their grandmother's isolated house to bury their twin, Yuliya—only to learn at the funeral that the body in the casket is Ulyana's own. The house has been keeping a second version of them alive in the old well, sustained by a lullaby the grandmother sang, and every photograph now shows an extra chair where the twin should sit. As the well refills with meltwater, the household's dead begin demanding the song's final verse, which binds one twin to the dark and frees the other. Ulyana must choose between singing their sister home and singing themselves under, and in the end they sing the verse together, split down the middle, so that neither twin is wholly buried—and the house, cheated of a whole soul, begins to starve.
about_author: Wendell Vane is the pen name of a former rural coroner's assistant who spent six years cataloguing unclaimed effects in a county with more wells than streetlights. Their fiction has appeared in small-press anthologies, and 'Bell and Choir' is their first novel.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. At the funeral home, Ulyana lifts the casket lid and finds their own face, five years older than their memory of it. The director insists paperwork doesn't lie; the grandmother's house on the hill does. Emotional beat: vertigo—the ground truth of identity pulled out from under them.

chapters.title: Housekeeping for the Dead
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. They move into grandma's house to sort the estate, finding dust arranged in patterns, two toothbrushes wet in the cup, and a chair pulled up to every table that no one admits to moving. Beat: dread disguised as domestic routine.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Developing the funeral photographs, Ulyana discovers every image from the past five years contains an empty chair facing the camera—including photos taken in the city, hundreds of miles away. Beat: the haunting was never local; it followed them.

chapters.title: Neighbor with a Lantern
chapters.summary: Deacon Hale's POV. The nearest neighbor, an old man who tends the church bell, watches Ulyana arrive and remembers when there were three Coldharbours, not two. He burns something in his yard each night. Beat: the community knows and has chosen silence over truth.

chapters.title: What the Well Remembers
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Following wet footprints to the capped well behind the house, Ulyana hears humming below—Yuliya's voice, singing the lullaby but stopping short of the last verse. Beat: grief curdling into terror as the dead twin asks for help.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. In a locked bureau, Ulyana finds grandma's accounts: payments made across decades to someone called the Choirkeeper, and entries tallying verses learned against verses owed. The last entry reads 'one verse short.' Beat: the horror has bookkeeping; it is a debt.

chapters.title: Hale's Confession, Half of It
chapters.summary: Deacon Hale's POV. Pressed by Ulyana, Hale admits the village once drowned a wrongdoer in the well and bound her spirit with a binding-song; the Coldharbour twins' grandmother volunteered her family line to keep it fed. He refuses to say what the crime was. Beat: loyalty to the village vs. the truth he's withholding.

chapters.title: Singing Lessons
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The lullaby begins rising unbidden in Ulyana's throat; when they hum even a bar, objects in the house rearrange to make room for someone. They tape their mouth at night and dream in harmony. Beat: the temptation to belong to the song.

chapters.title: The Photograph That Moves
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. A photo of the twins as children now shows the extra chair occupied by a blurred figure that shifts closer each time Ulyana looks. Their reflection in the glass wears an expression Ulyana isn't making. Beat: the boundary between observer and observed dissolving.

chapters.title: Choirkeeper
chapters.summary: The Choirkeeper's POV (first appearance). A gaunt figure who lives in the church crypt explains the terms: the well refills at spring thaw, and whoever sings the final verse alone takes the other's place below. She offers to teach Ulyana the verse—for a price paid in memory. Beat: power offered as salvation, priced as self.

chapters.title: Yuliya Below
chapters.summary: Yuliya's POV, from inside the well. The buried twin describes five years of singing to stay anchored, watching through water and roots as Ulyana lived her life. She is not angry; she is patient, and that is worse. Beat: sympathy for the thing in the dark.

chapters.title: The Village That Looked Away
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Researching parish records, Ulyana uncovers what Hale hid: the drowned woman was innocent, condemned by the village to protect a beloved son. The binding-song wasn't justice—it was a cover-up set to music. Beat: rage at lawless 'justice'; theme crystallizes.

chapters.title: Bell Tolling Backward
chapters.summary: Deacon Hale's POV. The church bell rings at midnight without being struck, and Hale knows the Choirkeeper is calling the village to renew its bargain. Some neighbors bring offerings; Hale brings nothing and feels his protection thinning. Beat: complicity cracking under pressure.

chapters.title: Split Voice
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Singing in their sleep, Ulyana wakes standing at the open well with rope-burned palms and mud to the knee. Yuliya's voice thanks them. Ulyana realizes the song is using their body whether they consent or not. Beat: loss of bodily sovereignty; stakes become immediate.

chapters.title: The Price of Forgetting
chapters.summary: The Choirkeeper's POV. She shows Ulyana what she took from others who bargained: a woman who forgot her children, a man who forgot his name. She reveals her own emptied face—she was the first Coldharbour to pay. Beat: corruption of power shown from inside the corrupter.

chapters.title: Thaw
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Ice breaks on the hills; the well level rises visibly day by day. The extra chair now sits at the foot of Ulyana's bed. Grandma's ledger pages begin turning themselves toward the final entry. Beat: countdown pressure; dread becomes arithmetic.

chapters.title: Hale's Last Truth
chapters.summary: Deacon Hale's POV. Dying, Hale gives Ulyana the missing piece: the final verse can be sung by two voices in unison, splitting the debt between them—but no one has ever dared share a grave. He begs forgiveness with his last breath. Beat: the mechanism of escape revealed too late to feel safe.

chapters.title: Offering at the Wellhead
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The Choirkeeper demands Ulyana choose by dawn, presenting it as mercy. Ulyana instead descends to the well mouth and speaks directly to Yuliya for the first time—not the song, just words: apology, anger, love. Beat: loyalty and truth finally face each other.

chapters.title: The Verse
chapters.summary: Alternating Ulyana/Yuliya POV. At moonset, both twins sing the final verse together—one above, one below—each carrying half the melody, half the debt. The well convulses; the Choirkeeper screams that a shared grave is not a grave at all. Beat: climax; defiance of the bargain's logic.

chapters.title: What Rose and What Stayed
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Dawn finds the well dry and the house ordinary. But Ulyana carries a coldness in the chest where Yuliya's half of the song settled, and sometimes their hands move without instruction. Beat: bittersweet survival—they won, but incompletely.

chapters.title: Chair, Empty
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Weeks later, the photographs show the extra chair again—now pushed back from the table, as if recently vacated. Ulyana sets a place for it anyway, learning to live with a guest who is also themselves. Beat: uneasy peace; the haunting domesticated but not ended.

chapters.title: Coda: Bell and Choir
chapters.summary: Deacon Hale's successor's POV. A new caretaker rings the morning bell and hears, beneath it, two voices finishing a song in perfect unison before falling silent. In the last photograph of the village, every porch has an extra chair. Beat: resolution with a lingering note—the debt deferred, the song waiting for the next singer.
